Aquifers - Ground water occurs in a number of aquifers which underlie Tracts II and III. These aquifers are parts of local, intermediate and regional flow systems. The water occurs in intergranular openings in both unconsolidated and consolidated rocks and in joints, fractures, and solution openings in consolidated rocks. Virtually all water in the coal bed aquifers is in fractures. Alluvium, colluvium, and the clinker material constitute the unconsolidated deposits. Consolidated rock aquifers and aquitards in the Tongue River member of the Fort Union Formation are the Rosebud-McKay overburden, the Rosebud-McKay coal bed, the coal interburden zone, the Robinson coal, and upper and low er sub-Robinson units (Westmoreland Resources 1975 1). The lower sub-Robinson unit is also referred to as the undifferentiated Fort Union. Detailed descriptions and physical characteristics of these aquifers are presented in Appendix D.
The aquifers in the Fort Union Formation are described by Van Voast and Hedges (1974, p. 3) as follows:
"The Fort Union aquifers are difficult to describe. The siltstone and sandstone beds have poor lateral continuity; they cannot be mapped or traced over large areas. The coal beds have a much greater continuity but have less predictible hydrologic characteristics. They transmit water by way of fractures in some locales; in others, they are so nearly impermeable that water is perched above them or confined below them. Because of the non-consistent nature of Fort Union aquifers in the area, they are best described as 'aquifer zones' rather than specific units."
Deeper aquifers are the Lebo Shale member of the Fort Union Formation and the combined Tullock member of the Fort Union Formation and Hell Creek Formation.
